s: was_attacked_by Gen. Buckner [during the Civil War] Brackett's battalion was the only Minnesota force engaged at Fort Donelson during its attack and surrender in February 1862. Capt. E.Y. Shelly's unit performed exhausting service to prevent Gen. Buckner from receiving reinforcements, and the regiment later returned to defend the fort against attacks in August 1862 and February 1863.

presents silk flag presented to the Second Minnesota [through its mayor] Louisville became the Second Minnesota's destination after its planned movement to Washington was changed. The regiment later returned there, where Mayor J.M. Dolph presented it with a silk flag in recognition of its conduct at Mill Springs.

Pittsburg Landing, on the Tennessee River, was the principal Union position and battlefield vicinity in the April 6–7 battle. Union troops and reinforcements arrived by steamer and used the landing and nearby river positions during the fighting. The First Minnesota battery arrived in late February 1862, fought there, and William Henry Acker was killed there.

Brackett's battalion was a military battalion of three Minnesota companies, mustered in September 1861. Initially assigned to Curtis horse and later the Fifth Iowa cavalry, it was the only Minnesota force engaged at Fort Donelson, then served in scouting, railroad protection, Tennessee campaigns, and Gen. Sully's Dakota campaign.

Printing and typesetting was Capt. E.Y. Shelly’s profession before and after military service. Historically overlapping with theater, it joined technical and editorial work with politics, publishing, and civic service. Territorial offices and newspapers relied on mobile printers and notable compositors, but the iron printer diminished composing rooms’ former sociability and informal intellectual exchange.

Territorial printers were a group of printers, reporters, editors, publishers, foremen, and type founders. Closely affiliated with editors, they worked and often slept in printing offices because hotels were scarce and economy mattered. Their composing rooms fostered debate, literary quotation, and sociability. The record lists many members, including Capt. E.Y. Shelly, and identifies a smaller set then known to survive.
James Mills came early to Minnesota, worked at the Pioneer office and its editorial department, then after the war returned to Pittsburgh as Pittsburgh Post editor-in-chief.
John P. Owens, a printer, first edited and published the Minnesotian with George W. Moore, then partnered with John O. Terry.
John O. Terry, St. Paul’s first hand pressman, partnered with John P. Owens to publish the Minnesotian, then long served as assistant postmaster and held trusted positions.

l: The decisive battle of Mill Springs, Novel-10146
s: The decisive battle of Mill Springs was a battle in Kentucky, part of the American Civil War and the first important Union victory in the Southwest after its outbreak. Led against Confederate commander Zollicoffer, with the Second Minnesota Infantry Regiment as a Union hero, it inflicted about 600 Confederate losses, cost 248 Union losses, captured twelve cannon, opened a route to East Tennessee, and forced Albert Sidney Johnston’s withdrawal.

commanded Sherman's division [Union division during the battle] William Tecumseh Sherman commanded a Union division whose position saw some of the hardest fighting on the first day. He was wounded slightly twice, had a ball pass through his hat, and lost several horses, while his resistance was important to the Union defense.

commands Second Minnesota Infantry Regiment [as commander of the First division] George H. Thomas commanded the First Division that included the Second Minnesota, the Eighteenth United States Infantry, and the Ninth and Thirty-fifth Ohio regiments. His troops began the Mill Springs campaign on January 1, 1862.

is_led_by George H. Thomas The Mill Springs campaign began on January 1, 1862, under George H. Thomas. The troops marched through rain, sleet, and mud before camping near Logan's Cross Roads and engaging the Confederate forces at Beech Grove.

is_located_near Beech Grove [eight miles north] Logan's Cross Roads was the Union camp where George H. Thomas's troops assembled before the battle. It lay eight miles north of Zollicoffer's entrenched Confederate camp at Beech Grove.

is_a Confederate camp [intrenched rebel camp] Beech Grove was the site of Zollicoffer's entrenched Confederate camp, located eight miles south of Logan's Cross Roads. Confederate forces withdrew from the area after the battle.

Bailie Peyton, a Confederate lieutenant and son of a prominent Union man in Tennessee, refused to surrender at the decisive battle of Mill Springs, shot Lieutenant Stout, was immediately killed, and had his sword captured by Lieutenant Tuttle.

Zollicoffer, a Nashville Confederate commander who had opposed Tennessee's secession, followed the state after it seceded, commanded forces at the decisive battle of Mill Springs, and was killed there when Colonel Fry shot him.

kills Zollicoffer [according to his own account] Colonel Fry of the Fourth Kentucky reported that he killed Zollicoffer during the battle. He described shooting the Confederate general in the breast after Zollicoffer's companion fired at him.

l: Union victory at Mill Springs, Novel-10146
s: An important Union victory, it broke up the Confederate right flank, opened a route into East Tennessee, helped force Albert Sidney Johnston's troops from Bowling Green to Nashville, and caused rejoicing among loyal residents.

was_killed_at The Great Battle of Pittsburg Landing [first day] Albert Sidney Johnston commanded the Confederate forces at Pittsburg Landing. He was killed during the first day's battle while attempting to induce a Confederate brigade to charge the enemy.

Kentucky was the setting for the Mill Springs campaign and battle, which loyal Kentuckians viewed as a victory over rebel invaders from Tennessee, Mississippi, and Alabama. Kentucky troops, including Wolford's First Cavalry and the Fourth Kentucky Infantry, were among the first to confront the invaders.

l: The Great Battle of Pittsburg Landing, Novel-10146
s: The Great Battle of Pittsburg Landing, also called Shiloh, was a two-day Civil War battle at Pittsburg Landing on April 6–7, 1862. Confederate forces attacked the Union Army of the Tennessee; the Army of the Cumberland under Buell reinforced it. The First Minnesota battery fought advancing Confederate forces for hours, notably at the Hornet's Nest, helping keep Union lines from being forced toward the Tennessee River. After Buell arrived, it was held in reserve on April 7. Union forces ultimately drove the Confederates from the field amid heavy casualties on both sides.

was_commanded_by Ulysses S. Grant [during the battle] The Army of the Tennessee, commanded by Ulysses S. Grant, was attacked at Pittsburg Landing before the arrival of much of Don Carlos Buell's army. It resisted the Confederate assault and, after receiving reinforcements, helped drive the enemy toward Corinth.

was_commanded_by Don Carlos Buell [during the battle] The Army of the Cumberland, under Don Carlos Buell, was expected to join Grant's forces at Pittsburg Landing. The text states that critics believed Buell could have made the junction earlier and thereby reduced the Union loss of life.
Henry W. Halleck suspended Grant, assumed command of Union forces at Pittsburg Landing after the battle, placed Grant second, built unused fortifications, and was then ordered to Washington.

commanded Union division [arrived from Crump's Landing after nightfall] Lew Wallace brought 5,000 Union troops from Crump's Landing after nightfall on the first day. His division appeared on the Confederate left during the retreat and was strongly reinforced on the second day.

The Union forces were positioned near the Tennessee River at Pittsburg Landing. The Confederate plan was to reach the river after defeating Grant, but gunboat fire and Union resistance prevented that result.

is_a old log church [near the hardest fighting] The Church of Shiloh was an old log church about three miles from Pittsburg Landing. Some of the hardest fighting occurred in its vicinity, giving the battle its alternate name, the Battle of Shiloh.

l: Grant's command of the Army of the Tennessee, Novel-10146
s: Grant's command of the Army of the Tennessee was threatened before the battle when Halleck suspended him, but a restoration order arrived before Grant learned of the suspension. After the battle, Halleck placed Grant second in command until Grant later received command of the Department of West Tennessee.

was_subject_to allegations of drunkenness [during the battle controversy] Grant's military reputation was damaged by accusations that he was drunk, absent from the battlefield, and unprepared for the Confederate attack. The text rejects those claims by describing his active direction of the battle and noting that his army made a firm resistance.

was_attributed_to Don Carlos Buell [slow advance to the Tennessee River] Buell's delayed reinforcement was criticized as a possible cause of the Union army's terrible first-day losses. The text states that Buell was at Columbia on March 19 and required nineteen days to reach the Tennessee River, although his troops eventually reinforced Grant.

numbered 13,047 [1,754 killed, 8,408 wounded, and 2,885 missing] The Union casualties in the two days of fighting were reported as 1,754 killed, 8,408 wounded, and 2,885 missing. The first day also saw approximately 2,200 men captured with Prentiss and about 6,000 inexperienced recruits flee toward the river.

was_alleged_during The Great Battle of Pittsburg Landing [charge described as false by the narrative] Grant's alleged drunkenness was one of several charges made against him after the battle. The text states that he was instead in the saddle from early morning until late at night, directing Union divisions despite severe pain from a sprained ankle.

The First Minnesota battery was a light artillery organization organized at Fort Snelling in fall 1861 under first captain Emil Munch. After receiving equipment in St. Louis, it joined Grant's army through Prentiss' division and was transferred there before Pittsburg Landing. The only Minnesota organization engaged in that battle, it helped hold the Hornet's Nest, drove off rebel batteries, suffered losses, and was commended. It later served in the Vicksburg and Atlanta campaigns and the March to the Sea.

Emil Munch was made the first captain of the First Minnesota battery when it was organized at Fort Snelling in the fall of 1861. During the Battle of Pittsburg Landing, his horse was shot in the head and he was wounded in the thigh, preventing him from continuing in the battle; Lieutenant Pfaender then took command.

is_a assassination The assassination was announced over the wires on the morning of April 15, 1865, after Lincoln was shot by an assassin. It caused nationwide grief and condemnation and was remembered as an especially appalling event.
President Lincoln’s death, caused by an assassin’s bullet shortly after Richmond’s fall and Lee’s surrender, ended his life and led to nationwide mourning and church commemoration.
House of Hope church on Walnut Street became a mourning-filled house of sorrow after Lincoln’s assassination, holding a crowded, solemn memorial service for Abraham Lincoln.

Frederick A. Noble, pastor of House of Hope church, is portrayed as an eloquent, learned, fearless, forcible, and aggressive divine. During the Rebellion he supports the Union with stirring war addresses, admires Abraham Lincoln, and after Lincoln’s death delivers an emotional memorial sermon praising Lincoln and eulogizing Seward.
House of Hope congregation is an intensely patriotic group, with many members serving at the front; Lincoln’s death brings a household-like loss and widespread weeping at a memorial service.
The Union cause is believed by Frederick A. Noble to be just and destined for final triumph, sustaining his support for vigorous war prosecution.
An assassination conspiracy targets the president, vice president, and cabinet; conspirators kill Lincoln, while Secretary of State Seward survives.
John Wilkes Booth fires the bullet that kills Abraham Lincoln at the Civil War's end; his act is remembered as a horrific crime.
Frederick A. Noble’s House of Hope church sermon after the assassination recounts Lincoln’s early history and presidential achievements, condemns the killing, and eulogizes William H. Seward.

A solitary voyageur journeys north on the Mississippi River bearing peace and goodwill to red men, then returns to St. Paul more than eighty years later, aged, sees transformation and Okon dominance, and departs in anguish.

Robert A. Smith is portrayed allegorically as a young paleface foretold by a dusky maiden to become mighty chief of the great city. The later scene identifies him as St. Paul’s 1902 mayoral candidate, ruling with Okon support and dispensing offices.
An astrologer, the dusky maiden foretells Robert’s future, gives him an elixir promising lasting life and power over enemies, and counsels caution, withdrawal from danger, and favoring the Okons.

The Okons, lineal descendants of sea kings from the bogs of Tipperary, aid Robert A. Smith when city requirements outgrow him, then in the later city they and their followers control every office within his gift.

control offices [within the gift of Robert A. Smith] The followers of the Okons are to receive and retain offices through Robert’s patronage. In the later city, they possess every office within the paleface’s gift alongside the Okons.

has magnificent building [in its midst] The dusky maiden predicts that a great city will eventually be built on the ground Robert surveys. When the voyageur returns, it has become a populous and technologically advanced metropolis with enormous buildings and rapid transportation.

houses Robert A. Smith [as high and mighty ruler] A magnificent building erected through the generosity of the people stands in the midst of the transformed city. Robert, supported by the Okons, rules from it.

The dusky maiden instructs Robert to arrange the offices within his gift so that the Okons and their followers remain securely established. In the later city, the Okons and their followers occupy every such office.

l: prophecy of the dusky maiden, Novel-10146
s: is_fulfilled_by Robert A. Smith [as ruler of the great city] The prophecy states that Robert will become the long-reigning chief of a great city, avoid firm political commitments, and depend on the Okons and their followers. The later events are presented as its fulfillment, including Robert’s mayoral campaign in 1902 and the Okons’ control of the offices.

l: city government and political patronage, Novel-10146
s: is_controlled_by Okons [with followers of the Okons] The city government is portrayed as centered on Robert, who preserves support by avoiding decisions that might alienate opposing parties and by relying on the working majority to resolve controversies. Political patronage keeps the Okons and their followers in all offices within his gift.

produces great city [over more than four score of years] When the voyageur returns after more than eighty years, the former wilderness has become a vast modern city. Cultivated fields, steamers, steam-powered and electrically powered transportation, gigantic buildings, and a large population replace the earlier frontier setting.

The narrator, about twelve and living in a small northern Pennsylvania village, secretly attends a spelling match despite being deemed too young, spells “phthisic,” defeats four schools, and gains an established reputation as a champion speller.
A small northern Pennsylvania village, mountainous and sparsely settled, lacks railroad and telegraph; its residents’ prosperity and intellectual opportunities are limited before later improvements.

School districts generally offered reading, writing, and arithmetic as principal studies for up to six months yearly when able; older children missed summer school to cultivate soil, and four districts joined a grand spelling contest.

participates_in spelling match [as one of four schools in the grand contest] The narrator's school participated in the grand spelling contest against three other schools. It was declared to have furnished the champion speller after the narrator correctly spelled "phthisic."

l: schoolmaster from the narrator's district, Novel-10146
s: A schoolmaster teaches the narrator’s district school and, at a spelling contest, notices the narrator apart, calls them one of its best spellers, pronounces words, expects “phthisic,” and confirms the correct spelling.

are_ranked_by spelling ability [in the order of their reputation as spellers] The pupils and scholars from four schools lined up for the spelling contest according to their reputations as spellers. One after another, the older scholars were eliminated by simple words and then by "phthisic," leaving the narrator as the only contestant standing.
A Saturday-night spelling match at a country crossroads brings four schools together, including other districts, and ends with the narrator's school established as winner.
Phthisic is a difficult word absent from the spelling book, used to eliminate contestants; the narrator, familiar with it, correctly spells it to finish the match.

is_won_by our school [among four districts] The spelling championship among the four districts went to the narrator's school because the narrator outlasted the other contestants. The narrator was thereafter recognized as the champion speller and was no longer placed last in the line.

Frank Moore, born in Tioga county, Pa., came to St. Paul and began work for the Minnesotian on April 17, 1858, at fifteen, doing errands, deliveries, and other printer’s-devil duties. He joined the Pioneer Press when it absorbed the Minnesotian in 1861, except for Civil war volunteer service, and continued after the 1874 merger. By sixty-five, he had led the composing room for about forty years and was noted for loyalty, devotion, and efficiency.

l: fiftieth anniversary of Frank Moore's connection with the paper, Novel-10146
s: is_celebrated_by informal dinner honoring Frank Moore [at Magee's] Frank Moore’s fiftieth anniversary of connection with the Pioneer Press was celebrated on April 17, 1908, with an informal dinner at Magee’s attended by a dozen old employees of the paper.

is_led_by Frank Moore [for about forty years] Frank Moore served as superintendent of the Pioneer Press composing room for about forty years. He continued to fill the position efficiently at age sixty-five, as the newspaper grew from its early beginnings into a large modern operation.

This document is a descriptive and travel account of Morocco, its neighboring Tunisian Sahara, and the Jereed, combining social observation, political history, geography, commerce, and personal narrative. It begins with Morocco’s Jewish communities, especially at Mogador and in the Atlas, describing changing treatment, customs, beliefs, marriage, and vulnerability, including Mogador’s later devastation. It then traces the Maroquine dynasties to the ruling Shereefs, whose descent from Ali and Fatima underpins their religious and political authority. Muley Suleiman and Muley Abd Errahman are central figures, alongside discussions of slavery, European relations, and British influence. The middle chapters survey Morocco as an empire of uncertain bounds and uneven imperial control. They describe its peoples, Berbers, Arabs, Moors, Jews, and Blacks, its Atlas Mountains, climate, products, mines, trade, horses, tribal regions, ports, coastal towns, imperial cities, oases, and caravan routes. Fez, Mequinez, Morocco, and Tafilett receive particular attention, while the text repeatedly emphasizes local tribal independence, uncertain population figures, neglected resources, and perceived urban decline. The Figheegh oasis cluster illustrates both productive irrigation and conflict over water. The narrative then shifts to events at Mogador, where disputes involving Jewish youths and Moors occur and the Governor states that the Sultan will resist anti-slavery appeals unless compelled by superior force. It moves to Tunisian territory, explaining the date-palm economy of El-Jereed before following Captain Balfour, Richard Reade, and Sidi Mohammed, Bey of the Camp, on an expedition toward Kairwan, Ghafsa, Toser, and Nefta. Their journey records the Bey’s camp and administration, justice and bastinado, saints, tribute collection, hunting, ruins, springs, oasis agriculture, date harvesting, waterworks, and harsh weather. Sheikh Tahid’s imprisonment, sale of his gardens, and release illustrate the Bey’s fiscal power. The travelers finally return to Tunis, and the narrator leaves Mogador on the Renshaw schooner, reaching England after a month of gales. An appendix recounts the French bombardment and capture of Mogador in August 1844, the flight of authorities and residents, the sacking and burning by wild tribes, the escape of European residents, and severe losses suffered by Jews and other inhabitants. Notes further distinguish Shereefs from Marabouts and summarize Barbary’s peoples, places, geography, and traditions.

Morocco is an independent Mussulman kingdom in North Africa, part of Barbary and ruled by the Shereefian dynasty, whose princes claim descent through Ali and Fatima. Also called El-Gharb, Mogrel-el-Aksa, and sometimes the Country of the Sultan Muley Abd Errahman, it is bounded by the Mediterranean and Straits of Gibraltar in the north, the Atlantic in the west, southern deserts and the Sahara in the south, and Algeria, the Atlas, and Tafilett in the east. Its history is presented through Saracen-founded monarchies, civil war after Yezeed’s death, later rule by Muley Suleiman and Muley Abd Errahman, and relations with European powers involving diplomacy, trade, piracy, slavery, and treaties. The country is a large central ridge, crossed northeast to southwest by the Atlas Mountains, with slopes toward the Atlantic and rivers toward the Sahara. Its climate and soil resemble Spain and Portugal: northern provinces are more like Spain, while southern ones have less rain and more desert heat. Although it has extremes of heat and cold and much desolate, uncultivated land, it is described as among Africa’s healthiest countries. Large rivers are numerous but not navigable far inland; northern rivers are short and full, and southern rivers are longer and often nearly dry. The coast has few, poorly protected ports. Agriculture centers on wheat and barley, with irrigated vegetables, fruits, forests of Argan and oak, cork, cedar, date-palm, and palmetto. Resources include silver, copper, sulphur, salt, amethyst, and materials used for fine leathers. Morocco is divided into Fez, central Morocco, Tafilett, and Sous, as well as natural regions and central districts. Its society includes Jews, Moors, Berbers, Arabs, Amazirghs, Touaricks, Israelites, and Renegades, under unequal social and religious conditions. The city of Morocco, or Maraksh, built by Yousel-Ben-Tashfin at the foot of the Atlas, is a southern capital and Sultan’s residence with mosques, markets, gardens, caravan trade, and visible decay. Commerce exports agricultural products and raw materials but is said capable of greater growth under more liberal government and lower duties.

Mogador is a Moroccan coastal port, with an isle, water-port, consulates, merchants, a Governor, and a European Jewish community. It is governed by Moorish authority and hosts European merchants, British consular authorities, European residents, and Jews whose social life increasingly overlaps with European society. Commerce is central, yet merchants are tightly controlled by the Moroccan government and at times barred from visiting vessels or supervising the stowing of their goods despite treaty provisions. It is also a setting for disputes involving Jewish merchants, London Jew-boys, the British Consul, and the Governor, and for anti-slavery tracts and a circular distributed among British merchants. Its gravest episode is the French bombardment of 13 August 1844: batteries were silenced, the Governor and most inhabitants fled, wild tribes sacked and burned the city, and the Jewish community endured massacre, plunder, homelessness, and starvation, leaving Mogador largely ruined and unoccupied.

Mogador Jewesses are Jewish women settled in Mogador, prominent in European society as belles attending balls. Exempt from walking barefoot, they cross religious and cultural boundaries through European dress and husbands.

Moroccan Jews historically endured Moorish oppression, humiliation, violence, restrictions, and unequal justice, including slavery and plunder; their condition reportedly improved over the preceding half century as some entered European society, adopting its clothing and habits and gaining manners and respectability.
European merchants mixed with Jews from London, Gibraltar, and Marseilles, helping form Mogador's European society.

Moors are described as having oppressed Jews, including by violence, legal favoritism, and social humiliation. During the bombardment of Mogador, Moorish rabble plundered Jewish houses and stripped Jewish women, while Moorish men also practiced early marriage, polygamy, and the drinking of white brandy.

Berbers are a group also called Moors or Barbarians in Roman usage, comprising many tribes and subdivisions, including Amayeegh, Kabyles, Aoures, Shelouh, Shouwiah, and Touarichs. Many live in Atlas and other mountains, while Arab tribes are said to occupy plains. They are portrayed as North Africa’s indigenous peoples or as descendants of the Getulians, resisting Roman and Arab conquerors and often retaining political independence. They protect certain Atlas Jewish communities and share a mountaineer way of life with them, but also join Arab tribes in plundering Mogador and fleeing Moors. In Rif and Garet they herd animals, use forests and other resources, and engage in market disputes under loose Sultan control. They founded Mequinez through Meknasab, built or inhabited several towns, and were feared by escaping Europeans during further plundering. Their present divisions differ from five ancient principal tribes.

The Berber race includes the Amayeegh and Shelouh varieties in Morocco. Chiefly mountain-dwelling, its members may be hard to distinguish from Arabs or Moors in urban life. Shelouhs form a major southern population, inhabiting places including Dimenet, Fronga, and Tagawost and living or trading with Moors and Jews.

Atlas Jews are dispersed through the Atlas ranges, living with quasi-independence under protecting Berber chieftains. They bear arms, speak Shelouh, dress like mountaineers, keep their own sheiks for domestic matters, and rarely go to plains or cities. They communicate through mountain networks, follow Berbers, regard Moroccan Jews as heretics, and are described as Caraaites.

describes Moroccan Jews [as oppressed under Moorish rule] Ali Bey described Jews as suffering continual disputes, violence, legal discrimination, forced removal of shoes, and restrictions on movement. He reported that Jews considered themselves slaves of the Sultan and compensated themselves for mistreatment by cheating Moors.

Muley Suleiman was Sultan and Emperor of Morocco. Proclaimed Sultan at Fez in the north during the civil war after Yezeed’s death, he became Sultan of the whole empire following Muley Hisham’s retirement. Described as a good and patriotic prince, he maintained peace and tranquility, stayed neutral during European wars, and cultivated peace with Europe. His most beneficent act toward European nations was abolishing Christian slavery in his States; he also exempted Mogador Jewesses from removing their shoes at mosques. He chose and declared his nephew Muley Abd Errahman, previously excluded because of youth, as legitimate hereditary successor. He died on 28 March 1820, about age fifty, and Abd Errahman succeeded him.

l: Muley Abd Errahman, Travels in Morocco
s: Muley Abd Errahman is a Shereefian prince and Sultan, the eldest son of Muley Hisham and nephew of Muley Suleiman. Suleiman chose and declared him legitimate hereditary successor instead of his own children. Portrayed as frugal, pacific, and generally not bloodthirsty, he consolidated imperial authority and preserved internal quiet with his vizier Bouseilam, though he was accused of avarice, confiscations, and imprisonments. He had three harems, used the Imperial parasol, and had sons governing Fez and Rabat.

The unit portrays Jewish religious and communal life through Passover, Tabernacle, and wedding festivals, Sabbath observance, and Jewish marriage customs. It also states that Jews in Mahometan countries were occasionally permitted to have four wives.

l: religion of the Atlas Jews, Travels in Morocco
s: The religion of the Atlas Jews differs from Jewish religion in the Pentateuch's order and law, resembles Caraaites, names the Supreme Being Shadai, lacks Ezra and Christ, and has a written law omitting the deluge and recounting Ishmael.

The Atlas Mountains are the principal heights of the Barbary region and Morocco’s central great mountain chain, called the Deren by natives and Dyris or Derem by ancient and modern aborigines. They extend across Morocco from northeast to southwest, from the Algerian frontier toward Cape Gheer, while records also place their broader span from Tripoli to Santa Cruz and from Cape Noun toward the Great Syrte. Their highest point is Miltsin, more than 15,000 feet above sea level; their greatest heights are in Morocco, especially east of Morocco and southeast of Fez, before diminishing eastward through Algiers, Tunis, and Tripoli. The range shapes Morocco’s climate, rivers, forests, minerals, water supply, fertile valleys, and routes south. It separates northern regions from the southern quasi-Saharan region and contains Berber settlements, including quasi-independent tribes beyond much of the Sultan’s authority. Its snowy ridges shelter Shelouh Jews and frame towns, districts, and Tafilett.

Tangier is a Moroccan port and a place in Barbary, strategically important to England as a former garrison and control point for the Herculean Straits. It marks the western extent of the Rif, with Tetouan southeast and the northern intermediate zone running toward Mogador. Its residents included Jews whom the Emperor forced to retain black turbans after some returned from Gibraltar in European dress. Tangier’s commerce was overwhelmingly tied to Gibraltar: in 1856 it imported British and foreign goods, exported to British and foreign ports, and supplied Gibraltar with cattle and provisions. England might seek it again in war.

Gibraltar is the European Pillar of Hercules, opposite the African pillar and Ceuta across the Straits of Gibraltar. It was conceded to England by the peace of Utrecht, with arrangements for provisioning its garrison. Tangier became its principal trading partner, sending cattle, poultry, eggs, flour, and other provisions; about 3,000 cattle annually went at a fixed duty, with roughly 2,000 more at higher rates. Monkeys were fancifully said to travel beneath the straits.

Fez is an ancient city and, historically, an independent kingdom; it is also described as the capital of the realm of Fez, the western royal court, and a leading city of Morocco. Separated from Morocco by the river Bouragrag, the kingdom once extended eastward to the gates of Tlemsen and is identified in a modern division with the northern kingdom of Fez. The city’s chief importance lies in learning, religion, wealth, industry, and commerce: it has old and new sections, hundreds of mosques, schools, markets, El-Karoubin, the formerly celebrated University of Fez, and Al-Kaisseriah. Its caravans travel annually to Timbuctoo and Mecca, while its manufactures include woollen haiks, silk handkerchiefs, slippers, shoes, and red felt caps. Though once powerful, its walls and defenses are decayed. Its population is uncertain, estimated from about thirty thousand to eighty-eight thousand or more, with fifty thousand considered probable. During a succession conflict, Muley Suleiman was saluted as Emperor there. Its foundation and full early history remain disputed or unknown.

Tunis is a regency of the Port of Tunis, ruled by an hereditary Bey, where severe punishments are rare. Nearly its entire surface is covered with Roman, Christian, and Moorish aqueducts. It is a starting point for journeys: tourists left it, sent baggage to Giovanni, obtained supplies there, and returned from the march. It supplied water for the Bey by camel and was the source of his extensive camel holdings, including animals exported to Sicily. Its commerce passed through Nefta toward the Sahara, and Dutch tiles from Tunis appeared there. The Bey’s decree gave Jews equal rights and privileges with other subjects. Tunis also had markets, Bardo ceremonies, Ghamart near Carthage, and sacrifices during drought and a frigate’s return.

l: French bombardment of Mogador, Travels in Morocco
s: A military bombardment beginning 13 August 1844 after Moorish gunfire, the French attack lasted about twenty-eight hours, inflicted heavy Moorish losses and few French casualties, and brought severe suffering to Jewish communities through massacre, plunder, ruin, starvation, and flight.

l: Mogador sack and destruction, Travels in Morocco
s: The sack and destruction of Mogador unfolded as French forces attacked from outside and plunder began within after Moorish authorities and people fled. Wild tribes, Moorish rabble, Berbers, and Arabs attacked and looted residents, especially Moroccan Jews, their homes, women, possessions, and records, leaving Mogador in ruins.

permits four wives [under privilege granted in Mahometan countries] Jewish polygamy is portrayed as rare and disorderly. One Jewish silk-merchant in Tunis had four wives whose household was marked by rivalry, quarrelling, neglect of the older wives, and the overattention of all four women to their only child.
Early marriage in Mogador involves girls marrying as young as nine, commonly at ten or eleven, including one nine-year-old wed to a man over fifty.

treat_marriage_as sale and barter [among Jewish and Moorish communities] Marriage customs among Jews and Moors are presented as arrangements of sale and barter rather than love. Engagements may be broken over the value of household goods, and wealthy older men are said to be preferred over handsome and amiable young men.

l: female beauty and obesity, Travels in Morocco
s: Female obesity is a Moorish beauty standard: before marriage, betrothed girls are forcibly fed and kept from exercise to enlarge their lower bodies, with enormous women considered especially attractive.

White brandy is a stimulant of immorality and intoxication in Moroccan society, produced and distributed by Moroccan Jews despite punishment, consumed by Moors as not grape juice, and troubling Jewish families on the Sabbath.

France is a European power entering relations with Morocco shortly after England, sending flags to Moroccan ports in 1555 under Francis I and gaining influence while England occupied Tangier. It later seeks peace, is linked to protection of a Jewish former consul, and may aid Moroccan Jews. Its influence and intervention are presented as potentially awakening energies and reconstructing declining royal cities amid Fez hostilities.

England could assist Moroccan Jews through governmental action, occupied Tangier during Anglo-Moorish struggles, expanded Moroccan influence and trade, then strengthened them after Trafalgar and Napoleon’s fall through treaties on peace, piracy, and subjects.

terminate_in Shereefian dynasty [historical succession] The Maroquine dynasties are listed as the Edristees, Fatamites, Zuheirites, Moravedi, Almohades, Merinites, Oatagi, and Shereefs. They succeeded one another from the Edristee accession in 789 until the Shereefs became the reigning dynasty.

The Shereefian dynasty is Morocco’s reigning southern Shereef dynasty, originating from a family near Medina in Arabia. It gained control through successive usurpations and divided into the Hoseinee and Fileli (El Fileli or Tafilett) branches; the latter became the present ruling line. Its rulers must sometimes favor Fez while facing restless tribes and rival political centers.

The Shereefs are a dynasty and family of descendants of the Prophet, profoundly venerated by true Mussulmen. Originating in and inhabiting Tafilett, including a small fortified town where many royal family members live in modest or impoverished conditions, they form a southern African branch distinct from the Shereefs of Fez. They claim the Moorish imperial throne and are presented as Mussulman sovereigns whose rulers exercise inviolable Shereefian privileges. Their authority combines regal and sacerdotal elements, though they are not strictly priests. Having once possessed the throne, they are jealous of the Marabouts; their court also defended slavery through Islamic scripture and tradition.

Islam is presented as permitting slavery and the slave trade through the Koran and traditions, while barring sale or transfer of a Muslim, the sacred misshaf, or a young person to an unbeliever. It is credited with unifying North Africa through religious homogeneity and removing notions of human sacrifice. The Shereefian sultans claim especially strong leadership through descent from Ali and Fatima. In Morocco, Islam binds diverse populations and extends the Sultan’s influence, while non-Muslim enemies can unite hostile tribes.

Abd-el-Kader is a highly revered marabout warrior and an object of enthusiasm among Mussulmen across North Africa, especially Morocco. Though he combines princely and sacerdotal authority like the Shereefs, he is not of the Prophet’s family and therefore could not dethrone the Shereefian dynasty. After withdrawing from Algeria, he sought refuge among Rif tribes, resisted the Imperial government for months, and finally chose pitched battle with the Sultan.

Muley Hisham, father of eldest son Muley Abd Errahman, disputed succession after Yezeed’s death, was proclaimed Sultan in Morrocco and Sous, retired to sanctuary in 1795, soon died, and was succeeded by Muley Suleiman.

Sidi Mohammed, Bey of the Camp, leads an expedition from the Bardo toward the Jereed, commanding its forces while honoring shrines, hunting, greeting divisions, receiving officers, and kindly hosting tourists; he dines alone, does not smoke tobacco, and is succeeded by Muley Yezeed.

Tafilett is a group of fortified towns and villages on the south-eastern side of the Atlas, always united to Morocco. Anciently called Sedjelmasa until 1530, it is the country and birthplace of the Shereefs, with places inhabited entirely by them and an area especially appropriated to the royal and Imperial family. The present Shereefian branch extended authority from Tafilett over the provinces of Morocco. It contains Ghourlan, is a date-country, and serves as a major market and Sahara caravan rendezvous. Its conjectural population is ten thousand; it also receives exiled troublesome Imperial-family members and is reached by the road from Aghmat.

Mequinez, or Miknas, is a hilltop royal residence and city in the province of Fez, founded by Meknasab. In a well-watered, pleasant region, it is enclosed by triple walls and has twenty thousand to fifty thousand inhabitants. It contains much of the Imperial guard, royal treasures, a Spanish hospitium, and an elaborately decorated palace; its people are polished, kind, and hospitable.

Rabat, or Er-Rabat, is a large, densely populated, fortified modern city in Temsna, opposite Salee on the Bouragrag River. Built by Jakob-el-Mansour as Rabat-el-Fatah, it has walls, gardens, plantations, forts, and a mausoleum associated with Almanzor. Its mostly Spain-expelled Moors and three or four thousand Jews support interior and foreign trade.

is_united_to Morocco [occasionally, historically] Sous is a southern region containing towns such as Tagawost, Fedsi, Messa or Assah, Talent, and Shtouka. It has fertile areas, trade with the Sahara and Timbuctoo, divisions among Shelouhs, Moors, and Jews, and districts that are sometimes nearly independent of Morocco.

North Africa is a region including Morocco and distinguished from the regencies of Tunis and Tripoli and from Algeria, an integral part of France. Its peoples include Berbers, Arabs, Moors, Jews, and Blacks; Berbers are described as aboriginal and mountain inhabitants, while Moors form much of the town and city population through mixture. It was successively inhabited or conquered by Libyans, Getulians, Phoenicians, Romans, Vandals, and Arabs, and is portrayed as religiously homogeneous under Islam. Numerous plains bear salt and nitre efflorescence, said to support apparently inexhaustible fertility despite little manure.
is_integral_portion_of France [under the Republic] The arrival of the French in Algeria is associated in the text with increased profligacy among Moorish women.
Moravedi is a Marabout dynasty, a family of priests that rose to consequence about 1050 and formerly ruled Morocco, retaining memory of sovereignty.
Muley Edris founds the Edrisiti dynasty and modern Fez, then is buried in a revered mausoleum where people invoke and venerate him.

Yezeed, son of Sidi Mohammed and a hereditary prince in the Shereefian line, was proclaimed Sultan at Salee three days after his father’s death. Partly descended through a renegade Irish maternal line, he was recognized by European consuls as a son of the Shereef. The records portray him as an exceptionally cruel tyrant whose principle was carnage, whose violent conduct and practical jokes helped cause civil war, and who made war on nearly the whole world except the English. After roughly 22 months of rule, he was mortally wounded by a poisoned arrow and died in February 1792. Though notorious for cruelty, he was buried with great solemnities at Kobah Sherfah; Muley Hisham succeeded him.

l: Graeberg de Hemso, Travels in Morocco
s: Consul-general for Sweden and Sardinia at Morocco, Graeberg de Hemso describes Moroccan towns and estimates Morocco's population at 8,500,000, considered exaggerated.

is_justified_by Islam [in the Sultan's correspondence with Mr. Hay] In the Shereefian lineage of Muley Suleiman, copied for Ali Bey by the Emper] The slave trade is defended in letters from the Sultan to Mr. Hay as a practice accepted since the time of the sons of Adam and confirmed by the Koran and the Sunnat. The correspondence states that Islamic law regulates the treatment, sale, emancipation, and religious transfer of slaves.

include Treaty of Fez of 1801 [signed at Fez on 14 June 1801] In the Shereefian lineage of Muley Suleiman, copied for Ali Bey by the Emper] The principal treaty discussed was signed at Fez on 14 June 1801 and confirmed on 19 January 1824 by Muley Suleiman. It addressed consuls, trade, disputes, punishment, religious renegades, and access to vessels, but the text argues that it required immediate revision because it gave excessive authority to the Emperor and insufficient security to British subjects.

l: Moorish imperial throne, Travels in Morocco
s: The Moorish imperial throne passed through a succession of dynasties before being held by the Shereefs. Muley Abd Errahman occupied it after Muley Suleiman and is credited with making imperial authority more solid and preserving the empire during his reign.
Mr. Willshire, a British Consul, is detained in Mogador during bombardment over liabilities, then escapes the sacked city with his wife and reaches the Warspite.

Salee, or Sala, is an ancient commercial and fortified city of Beni-Hassan on the right bank of the Bouragrag River near its mouth. Its small port is too shallow for large vessels. Captured by Alphonso the Wise in 1263, it returned to Moorish rule and later became a center of piracy; population estimates varied, with two or three thousand reported by a resident.

Dar-el-Beida, or Casa-Blanco, is a small Atlantic town in Shawiya, on the ruins of Anfa or Anafa, which the Portuguese destroyed in 1468 before building the town. It has a small port and spacious bay for large vessels, but only about 200 to 1,000 inhabitants.

In the Shereefian lineage of Muley Suleiman, copied for Ali Bey by the Emper] Muley Suleiman maintained neutrality while Christian powers in Europe were convulsed with war and cultivated peace with Europe. The text also discusses Morocco’s diplomatic intercourse with European princes and European efforts to influence Morocco.

l: Yezeed's succession crisis, Travels in Morocco
s: is_a civil war [following Yezeed's death] In the Shereefian lineage of Muley Suleiman, copied for Ali Bey by the Emper] After Sidi Mohammed’s death, Yezeed and Hisham disputed the succession, and Yezeed was proclaimed Sultan at Salee as the hereditary prince. Yezeed’s cruelties provoked civil war, and after his death the empire was divided among three pretenders before Muley Hisham and Muley Suleiman became the principal competitors.

l: Muley Suleiman's reign, Travels in Morocco
s: lasts_for a quarter of a century [approximately] In the Shereefian lineage of Muley Suleiman, copied for Ali Bey by the Emper] Muley Suleiman’s reign lasted about a quarter of a century. The text characterizes it as peaceful and prosperous, noting his just administration, neutrality in European wars, peaceful relations with Europe, and abolition of Christian slavery.

l: abolition of Christian slavery, Travels in Morocco
s: is_a act of Muley Suleiman [described as the most glorious and beneficent act of his reign for Europeans] In the Shereefian lineage of Muley Suleiman, copied for Ali Bey by the Emper] The abolition of Christian slavery in Muley Suleiman’s States is identified as the most glorious and beneficent act of his reign from the perspective of European nations.

In the Shereefian lineage of Muley Suleiman, copied for Ali Bey by the Emper] The text says that Moroccan rulers formerly subjected Christian captives to severe bondage, motivated partly by hostility toward Spain and revenge for injuries inflicted on the Moors. It credits Muley Suleiman with abolishing Christian slavery in his States.

governs British subjects [under Articles VII and VIII of the treaty] In the Shereefian lineage of Muley Suleiman, copied for Ali Bey by the Emper] The British-Moroccan treaties provide that disputes involving British and Moorish subjects are to be decided according to Moorish law in specified circumstances. The text criticizes this arrangement because it could expose British subjects to punishments imposed under the Moorish legal system.

l: British influence in Morocco, Travels in Morocco
s: becomes_supreme_after Trafalgar [following the fall of Napoleon] In the Shereefian lineage of Muley Suleiman, copied for Ali Bey by the Emper] British influence in Morocco grew after the peace of Utrecht and was strengthened by Trafalgar and the fall of Napoleon. British diplomacy sought to support Muley Abd Errahman’s pacific policy, counter French influence, and prevent French pretexts for invading Morocco.

are_exposed_to Moorish law [including potentially barbarous punishments under the treaty] In the Shereefian lineage of Muley Suleiman, copied for Ali Bey by the Emper] British subjects in Morocco were granted treaty protections concerning consuls, commerce, disputes, punishment, and access to vessels. The text argues that they remained exposed to Moorish punishments and uncertain justice, citing the imprisonment and attempted punishment of Mr. Saferty at Mogador.

Moors is a name used for inhabitants of Barbary and, in these records, especially the inhabitants and rulers of Morocco. They are described as living mainly in towns and cities, governing or possessing places including Arzila, El Araish, Mehedia, Salee, Rabat, and Dar-el-Beida, and as having retaken some coastal strongholds while leaving other fortifications weak or neglected. Accounts distinguish them from Arabs in some population classifications, while also giving varying accounts of their descent: Arabs in Spanish usage, people affected by the expulsion from Spain, or aboriginal Amazirghs. Their history is presented through conflicts, law, and treaties involving England, France, Spain, and other European powers. Social descriptions attribute religiously required bathing, particular building preferences, and contested accounts of cleanliness and conduct to them. One account reports contempt toward London Jew-boys and disagreement over abolition; another condemns feastday behavior as lascivious. In the military episode, they fire on French forces, fight effectively for two hours, then lose resolve after Omar Ei-Haj is killed, abandon the batteries, and flee. The closing notes reject an entirely uniform portrayal of them as dirty, lazy, inhuman, or indomitable while recording severe judgments about sacrifice and the origin of their name.

Arabs are a group associated with North Africa through conquest and later migration. Around the middle of the seventh century they invaded North Africa from Asia, fought Romans and indigenous Berbers, and later ruled Morocco. In the first years of the eighth century they invaded Spain; after expulsion from Spain, many refugees settled in Barbary and helped maritime cities grow. In Morocco they appear among mixed, nomadic populations, although their numbers are said to have been overstated relative to the aboriginal Amazirgh population. During the expedition, Arab troops, camp followers, and temporary welcoming groups supplied much of the supporting force. They joined the camp for inspection by the Bey, fired long guns, presented or lost horses to him, hunted, and displayed horsemanship. Records also describe their food, punishments for theft, women’s looloos, chiefs’ wives in camel palanquins, and ritual words spoken while slaughtering game.

l: Empire of Morocco, Travels in Morocco
s: The Empire of Morocco is a country in North Africa, also called El-Gharb, Mogrel-el-Aksa, and Blad Muley Abd Errahman. It has about six million people, a Sultan who heads the orthodox religion of Western Muslims, a military force, and annual commerce. Its effective dependent territory is estimated at 137,400 square miles, though its wider claims are often nominal or precarious. It includes Sous, Wadnoun, Rif, Atlas, and Tafilett, and claims Touat and Western Sahara. Its royal cities, El-Kesar, Mequinez, Fez, and Morocco, are commercially active but divided, decayed, and poorly defended.

l: Sultan of Morocco, Travels in Morocco
s: The Sultan of Morocco is a sovereign Shereef and head of the orthodox religion of the Mussulmen of the West, claiming authority across territories where direct power is often nominal. He has influence in Western Barbary and among Muslims in Central Africa, while Sous has no real power under him and Wadnoun offers only nominal acknowledgment and occasional presents. He uses religious titles and honors to divide chiefs and strengthen his position. Residing mainly at Fez, Mequinez, and Morocco, he maintains northern allegiance and restrains disaffected tribes, retreating to Morocco during difficult European relations. He refuses abolition of slavery unless superior Christian force compels it.

Rif is Morocco’s mountainous northern coastal region, stretching along the Mediterranean from the Moulwia to Tangier and bordering Habat. It includes Hashbat, Gharet, and Aklaia; is fertile and mineral-rich; is inhabited by warlike Berbers under precarious Sultan authority; shelters Abd-el-Kader after his retirement from Algeria; and is exceptionally dangerous to travel.

Barbary, also called the land of Barbary, is a North African region containing Morocco and including Algiers among the Barbary States. Its peoples were called Barbarians or Berbers by Romans and Arabs, giving rise to the term Barbary States; its inhabitants reject human sacrifice and may sacrifice animals to God or tutelar saints.

The Sahara is an immense sandy desert and a broader hot, dry region extending from the Atlantic toward Egypt, including the quasi-Saharan country south and southeast of the Atlas. It forms Morocco’s southern boundary, receives southeastern Moroccan slopes and streams that vanish in its sands, and begins beyond the Mulweeah in an extremely sterile tract. Its defining features are heat, drought, blowing sand, salt flats, sparse marshes, rocky hills, scattered elevations and mountain branches, and routes so difficult that hidden wells are essential. Yet it contains distant oases and settled districts: Touat, Agobli, Taoudeni, and the oasis cluster of Figheegh, with gardens, wells, agriculture, commerce, and mining. Morocco’s claimed sovereignty over some oases was little or not effectively exercised. Tatta and Akka gather caravans crossing the Great Desert. Travelers encounter the Sahara around the Jereed as an immeasurable ocean of sand; at Ghafsa, its sands begin to disappear and land becomes more fit for corn.

The Romans took control of Africa from the Phoenicians or Carthaginians and encountered indigenous peoples whom they called Moors, Berbers, or Barbarians. After being displaced by the Vandals, they later expelled or destroyed the Vandals, but eventually lost North Africa to the Arabs.

The Phoenicians successively invaded North Africa and established themselves on its shores around the foundation of Carthage, about 820 years before the Christian era. The Romans later received or wrested control of Africa from them.

Jews are present in many towns as merchants, artisans, traders, and sometimes farmers. The unit repeatedly describes Jewish quarters or populations in places such as Tefza, Tagodast, Dimenet, Tednest, Akka, Messa, and Ilirgh, and argues that Jewish commerce is important to the economic life of North African Muslims.

is_composed_of Berbers [chiefly mixed with Arabs and Blacks in Morocco, Sahara and Senegal] The Moorish population is concentrated mainly in Morocco’s towns and cities and consists of a mixture of many races, including descendants of Moors expelled from Spain. Europeans commonly call urban inhabitants Moors, although the population itself distinguishes more specifically between Arabs and Berber tribes.

l: Arab conquest of North Africa, Travels in Morocco
s: began about 650 [Arab invasion of Northern Africa] The Arab conquest of North Africa began around 650, when Arab forces from Asia attacked the declining Roman power. The Berbers initially submitted to the Arabs to escape Roman rule, then revolted and continued the struggle against their new conquerors.

l: Arab conquest of Spain, Travels in Morocco
s: began first years of the eighth century [conquering Arabs crossed from North Africa] The conquering Arabs crossed from North Africa into Spain in the early eighth century. Because they came from Mauritania, the Spaniards called them Moors, although the text states that they may have had little in common with the indigenous Moors of North Africa.

Elaeonderron Argan is a tree peculiar to southern Morocco, large, bushy, wide-spreading, lofty, branching, and broad-armed, sometimes as large as an oak. It bears olive-like fruit with an almond kernel crushed for rancid oil used instead of olive oil. It shades travelers; one celebrated ancient tree, said to have been planted by Okba, shelters many people and is admired for its grandeur.

Moroccan commerce centers on regional exports: northern Morocco sends cattle and grain, while southern Morocco sends gums and almonds. Additional goods include salt to Timbuctoo, alongside bark, skins, wax, wool, fish, and other products.

The Atlantic Ocean borders Morocco to the west and receives the country’s northwestern rivers. The Atlantic coast is characterized mainly by ridges of hills, and its ports offer poor protection from the ocean. The Atlantic Ocean borders the Moroccan towns described in this unit, including Arzila, El Araish, and the coastal settlements farther south. Its shores and roadsteads provide ports and anchorages, although many entrances are obstructed by sandbars, rocks, or shallow water.

produces rancid oil [from its crushed almond; commonly used as a substitute for olive-oil] Argan trees are bushy and large, sometimes reaching the size of wide-spreading oaks. Several argan forests grow near Mogador.

The date-palm is a male and female organism. The female requires communication with the male for good fruit. From shoots it bears in six or seven years; from stones in sixteen; reaches greatest vigour about thirty; and may bear for seventy years. At full vigour it produces fifteen or twenty date clusters annually and requires root water every four or five days. It yields leghma, branches, fibres, and hardened wood; tapped when fruit is scant. Fruitful palms may be destroyed in villages’ wars, though elsewhere in the Sahara they are spared.

l: climate and soil of Morocco, Travels in Morocco
s: The climate and soil of Morocco are described as similar to those of Spain and Portugal. Northern Morocco has a climate nearly like Spain’s, while the south has less rain and more desert heat but greater fertility for valuable commercial staples.

l: agriculture of Morocco, Travels in Morocco
s: Agriculture centers on wheat and barley in the plains, while vegetables and fruits are cultivated near towns. Irrigation sustains cultivation when rains cease or fail, allowing Southern European fruits and vegetables, as well as plants suited to Africa, to be grown successfully.

l: Moroccan mineral resources, Travels in Morocco
s: Moroccan mineral resources include especially abundant copper and deposits of gold, silver, lead, iron, tin, sulphur, mineral salt, antimony, saltpetre, and amethyst; most mines remain neglected or unworked because the government fears foreign interest, despite identified silver and copper areas.

Draha is a southern province containing Beni-Sabih, Tatta, and Akka, with caravan routes leading toward the Great Desert. Beni-Sabih, also called Moussabal or Draha, is its small but populated and commercial capital.

l: Northern kingdom of Fez, Travels in Morocco
s: The Kingdom of Fez includes places such as Seisouan, Wazen, Muley Driss, Taza, Oushda, Aghla, Nakhila, and Meshra Khaluf. Its districts contain fertile plains, commercial towns, sanctuaries, and areas where local religious or tribal authorities exercise considerable independence.

l: Eastern Province of Tafilett, Travels in Morocco
s: The Tafilett province was anciently called Sedjelmasa and later took the name Tafilett from an Arab immigrant associated with improved date cultivation. It contains several fortified towns and fertile level districts producing corn, fruits, vegetables, sheep, and woollen and silk manufactures.

has_nearby Kalat-el-wad [near its mouth or fifteen miles distant] The Moulwia, also called Mulweeah or Malwia, forms an important reference point for Morocco’s northern coast. The Rif is described as extending from the river’s mouth toward Tangier, and the Jafarine Isles lie near its mouth; Kalat-el-wad is situated near the river, although its navigability is unknown.

separates Salee [from Rabat] The Bouragrag River flows between Salee on its right bank and Rabat on its left bank before reaching the Atlantic. It is broad near the two cities and is presented as a natural line separating the more humid northern side from the higher and drier southern side.

Mazagran is an ancient, strong castle on a peninsula at the bottom of a spacious bay. Rebuilt by the Portuguese in 1506 as Castillo Real, it is also called El-Bureeja, meaning the citadel. Its thick walls and small port remain after the Portuguese abandoned it in 1769; it has two or three hundred inhabitants.

The Spanish possess the Jafarine Isles and the presidios of Melilla, Alhucemas, Penon de Velez, and Ceuta on the Moroccan coast. Their settlements are described as fortified or penal establishments, and their authority is portrayed as a remnant of Spain’s weakened power.
The text states that Moorish women had never been so profligate as since the arrival of the French in Algeria. Sultan Kaed had also distinguished himself against the French before Constantina.
The Jafarine Isles are three Spanish islands near the Moulwia’s mouth, opposite a small mainland town; recently fortified, their fortifications’ purpose is questioned.

Melilla is an ancient Carthaginian city near the cape Romans called Rusadir, capital of Garet. It has about 3,000 inhabitants and lies amid fertile country rich in minerals and honey; nearby, a Spanish presidio of the same name stands on a drawbridge-linked island.

Garet is a northern Moroccan province containing Melilla and extending through a rich and highly cultivated region. Like the Rif, it is inhabited by warlike Berbers over whom the Sultan’s authority is precarious.
Alhucemas is a small Spanish island presidio with about five or six hundred inhabitants, commanding its bay at the Wad Nechor mouth near Ed-Housh and the ruined ancient capital of Mezemma.

l: Penon de Velez, Travels in Morocco
s: Penon de Velez is a Spanish presidio-island and convict settlement opposite the mouths of the Gomera River, a strong but largely barren rock with about nine hundred inhabitants that receives fresh water from the mainland part of the year.

Gomera, or Badis, is a city on the mainland opposite Penon de Velez, identified with Parientina and possibly Acra of Ptolemy; reportedly once had 3,000 inhabitants, then was described as abandoned, inhabited only by serpents and hyenas.

Tetouan is a large, prosperous mercantile city in Hasbat, several miles inland from the Mediterranean and southeast of Tangier. Identified with Roman Yagath, it has 9,000–12,000 Moors, Arabs, Jews and Berbers, gardens and plantations, bazaars, a Jewish quarter, strong fortifications, and nearby Marteen port.

Ceuta, or Sebta, is an ancient city and fortress, formerly regarded as the capital of Mauritania Tingitana and identified with Esilissa of Ptolemy. It occupies a peninsula near Gibraltar, includes Monte-del-Acho and Gibel Zaterit, and has a small insecure port. Portugal conquered it in 1415; it later became a Spanish presidio, retained by Spain after Portugal recovered independence in 1640, with a garrison and free population.

l: Straits of Gibraltar, Travels in Morocco
s: separate Africa and Europe [at the pillars of Hercules] The Straits of Gibraltar are the maritime setting of Ceuta, which stands fourteen miles south of Gibraltar and nearly opposite it. The surrounding mountains are identified with the African Pillars of Hercules, facing Gibraltar as the European pillar.

l: Spain's North African presidios, Travels in Morocco
s: Spain's North African presidios include the settlements at Melilla, Alhucemas, Penon de Velez, and Ceuta, as well as the fortified Jafarine Isles. They are characterized as garrisons or convict settlements established on islands, peninsulas, or coastal strongpoints, and the text calls them of limited utility apart from their military or penal functions.

l: population statistics of Morocco, Travels in Morocco
s: Moroccan population statistics are presented as proximate, conjectural, uncertain, and often exaggerated because local resistance to counting and conflicting place estimates make reliable totals difficult. The records use discrepancies for towns and poorly known tribal populations to question estimates. Graeberg’s 8,500,000 is considered more plausible after a deduction of about two million, while Jackson’s nearly fifteen million is rejected as excessive.

l: Moroccan coastal towns and ports, Travels in Morocco
s: are of considerable interest [Mediterranean towns and ports] Moroccan coastal towns and ports on the Mediterranean are said to be important but poorly documented, apart from the Spanish presidios and well-known places such as Tetouan and Tangier. The unit describes Kalat-el-wad, Melilla, Alhucemas, Penon de Velez, Gomera, Tegaza, Tetouan, and Ceuta, noting their trade, fortifications, populations, bays, and varying degrees of accessibility.

l: Moroccan tribal administration, Travels in Morocco
s: Moroccan tribal administration rests primarily on tribes, with kaidats as European-style jurisdictions; tribal names shape districts, and the Sultan’s authority is weakest among Berber tribes of the Rif and Garet.

Arzila, or Asila, is an ancient Berber city in Hasbat on the naked Atlantic shore. Formerly called Zilia and Zulia under Roman rule, it has a small port, about one thousand people, and good tobacco from its surrounding country; its Portuguese fortifications are rapidly decaying under Moorish possession.

El Araish, also called Laratsh, is an Atlantic city and the capital and governor’s seat of Azgar, replacing ancient Lixus. Situated at the mouth of the Cos or Luccos River on a small promontory, it has Spanish-made fortifications and a secure but difficult port. It has about 4,000 people and a 500-troop garrison, was captured by the Spanish in 1610 and recaptured by Muley Ishmael in 1689, and produces cotton and exports cork and other goods.

Azgar is a district with El Araish as capital and governor's residence, inhabited chiefly by Beni-Arous; its name is linked to a powerful Touaricks tribe, and its environs contain vineyards and the Beni Arasis mountains.
Lixus, also called Liscas and Lixa, was an ancient city replaced by El Araish; five classes of its Phoenician coins depict grapes, corn ears, and fishes.

is rich and fertile [excepting a small desert part] Mauritania is described through the ancient Roman frontier and the fertile Atlantic region associated with Lixus. Strabo characterizes most of it as rich, fertile, well watered, and abundant in trees and other products, while Salee is identified as the farthest Roman city on the Atlantic coast of ancient Mauritania Tingitana.

Mehedia, also called Mamora or Nuova Mamora, is a maritime town in Beni-Hassan on the left bank of the Sebon River at its mouth, near the Mamora plain and forest. Built by Jakob-el-Mansour to defend the mouth, it was captured by Spanish in 1614, recaptured by Moors in 1681, and became a weak settlement with fishermen, a small garrison, and a crumbling castle.

Salee rovers were Moroccan pirates based at Salee and Rabat, forming a nearly independent military republic; bitter enemies of Christians, they intercepted British traders near Lundy Island and ranged as far as the British Channel.

Almanzor, also called Elmansor, was a famous, victorious Sultan who expelled the Moravedi from Spain, intended Rabat as his capital, and had an untenanted mausoleum there in a separate sacred quarter.

Azamor is an ancient city in Dukaila on the southern bank near the mouth of the Omm-er-Rbia River. Its fertile surroundings and Shebbel salmon trade matter most. Portuguese captured and fortified it in 1513, then abandoned it about a century later.

The Omm-Erbegh River passes near or through several settlements, including Meshra Khaluf, Tijijet, Bulawan, Soubeit, and Meramer. It provides fords and routes of travel, and the surrounding districts are often fertile and productive in grain and cattle.

Saffee, also called Asafee and formerly Soffia or Saffia, is an ancient city in Abda, built by Carthaginians near Cape Pantin. Its massive walls, summer roadstead, and European commerce matter most. With about one thousand inhabitants and uncultivated surroundings, it was captured by Portuguese in 1508 and abandoned in 1641.

l: Imperial Cities of Morocco, Travels in Morocco
s: is_a royal capitals [of the interior] The Imperial Cities of Morocco are identified as El-Kesar, Mequinez, Fez, and Morocco. They are described as royal or capital cities with important roles in administration, defense, commerce, religion, and learning, although all are said to be in decline.

El-Kesar is a fortified place in the Gharb, on the southern bank of the Luccos. Enlarged and beautified by Sultan Almansor around 1180 as a military magazine and rendezvous, it later declined, with narrow streets, ruined houses, inactive mosques, and four or five thousand souls. It hosted the Battle of the Three Kings in 1578.

l: Battle of the Three Kings, Travels in Morocco
s: The Battle of the Three Kings was fought at El-Kesar in 1578. It caused the deaths of Portuguese king Don Sebastian, Muley Moluc, and Portuguese nobility and chivalry; Muley Moluc died secretly in a litter to preserve Moorish courage.
Edris-Ben-Edris inherited the virtues and influence of his father, Edris Ben Abdalluh. He is credited with being the first bona-fide Mussulman sovereign of the Maroquine empire and with founding Fez.

contains library of antiquity at El-Karoubin [the existence of its ancient contents is presented as conjectural] El-Karoubin, also called El-Karouiin, is the most famous mosque of Fez and is supported by three hundred pillars. It is said to contain a celebrated ancient library with Greek and Latin authors and lost books of Titus Livy, although the text treats this claim as conjectural.

is_in_decline sere and yellow leaf [described as nearly defunct] Moorish civilization is portrayed as having entered a period of decline, with ruined cities, decaying fortifications, diminished learning, and weakened institutions. The text calls the royal cities the remnants of a once flourishing civilization and suggests that they may not recover without European reconstruction.

Wazen is a small unwalled city in Azgar and the Gharb, residence of the hereditary High Priest or Grand Marabout, whose substantial influence accompanies the district’s exemption from imperial tribute.

Muley Driss, also called Zawiat-Muley-Driss or Muley Edris, is a renowned city in the province of Fez, at the foot of the Terhoun Mountains northwest of Fez. It contains Edris’s sanctuary, lies in fertile country, and may occupy ancient Volubilis.

Taza, capital of the well-watered district of Haiaina, is a city on a river-surrounded rock. With 10,000 to 12,000 hospitable, commercially active inhabitants, it has spacious streets, a large mosque, good provisions, and commerce with Tlemsen and Fez.

Oushda is a northeastern frontier town and oasis in the Angad Desert, with 600 to 1,000 Moors and Arabs. A dilapidated fortress and garden walls protect clay houses, winding streets, and spring-irrigated gardens amid severe aridity.

are aboriginal population [of Morocco and the interior] The Amazirghs are described as an aboriginal population with their own elders, chiefs, and local institutions. Their mountain tribes frequently resist imperial authority, and their leaders may exploit conflicts between Morocco and European powers to avenge old grievances.

is_a decayed former capital [of Rhamna, now a village of about sixty families] Aghmat was formerly a great fortified city and the capital of Rhamna, but it has declined into a village inhabited by about sixty families, including a few Jews. It lies near the Atlas and a river of the same name in a fertile country of orchards and vineyards, and it was the first capital of the Marabout dynasty.

l: interior geography of Morocco, Travels in Morocco
s: is very obscure [especially in the South] The interior geography of Morocco, particularly in the south, is described as obscure, with multiple names and uncertain locations appearing on maps. The author selects places whose existence is considered certain while acknowledging discrepancies between sources such as Graeberg and Davidson.

l: Moroccan tribal independence, Travels in Morocco
s: causes weakness of the interior [through independent Amazirgh tribes] Many Moroccan districts and tribes operate with substantial independence from the Sultan. Religious leaders at Wazen and Tedda, Amazirgh chiefs, and communities in places such as Talent and Shtouka may collect no imperial tribute or govern themselves with only nominal submission to Morocco.

Figheegh, also called Figuiq, is a Saharan agglomeration of twelve villages, including Maiz, El-Wadghir, and Zenega. Governed by Sheikh Kebir, it is prosperous through palm plantations and date production, supplying western province of Algeria and trading with Fez, Tafilett, and Touat. Its gardens grow madder-root, tobacco, and barley; wheat comes from the Teli.

l: villages of Figheegh, Travels in Morocco
s: The twelve villages form a close cluster on the descent of Wal-el-Khalouf, connected and never more than a quarter of a league apart. Each has houses, a mosque, school, kady, and sheikh. Eternal strife among them, sometimes armed, has led to crenated walls and defensive towers; larger villages include Maiz, El-Wadghir, and Zenega.
Wal-el-Khalouf, the river of the wild boar, is dry except in winter; inexhaustible wells in its bed supply water distributed to gardens.

is_distributed_by clepsydra [among the gardens] Water is obtained from wells in the bed of Wal-el-Khalouf and distributed among the gardens by means of a clepsydra, a vessel that releases a measured amount over an hour. Its scarcity and distribution are the immediate causes of discord among the villages.

l: strife among the villages, Travels in Morocco
s: The villages are perpetually in conflict, sometimes taking up arms; water immediately causes disputes, and quarrels that reach bloodshed bring cruel destruction of productive date-palms.

l: people of Figheegh, Travels in Morocco
s: The people of Figheegh cultivate madder-root, tobacco, barley, fruit trees, and date-palms, and are skilled miners. Though engaged in severe warfare, they pursue commerce and industry, maintain relations with Fez, Tafilett, and Touat, and are generally prosperous.
London Jewish youths of the lower lemon-selling class resent Moors’ contempt; after one returns a Moor’s curse, the British Consul imprisons him.

is_a valley [three or four hours south of Mogador] Saneeates-Sultan, three or four hours' ride south of Mogador, is visited by the narrator and companions. Its valley contains the Garden of the Emperor, the river Wad-el-Kesab, sandy mounds, palmettos, Argan trees, and little cultivated land.

l: Garden of the Emperor, Travels in Morocco
s: is_also_called Saneeates-Sultan The Garden of the Emperor contains a well, a few fruit trees, and a celebrated Argan tree. European visitors carved their names into the bark of a fine fig tree there.

Argan forests in Morocco's arid country south of Mogador are linked to Moorish legends of enchantresses, magical springs, deceptive fruit, and wicked jinns, ending when a holy man breaks their enchantment.

l: Governor of Mogador, Travels in Morocco
s: Governor of Mogador is Sidi Abdallah Deleero, a Moorish Deputy-Governor commanding Mogador during a bombardment. He repeatedly prevents British and other European residents and detainees from leaving beforehand. He opposes abolition as the Sultan’s government’s position, says most Muslims in Morocco support slavery, and regrets he cannot aid anti-slavery work, believing argument will not persuade the Sultan.

supports abolition of slavery [believing a considerable number of Moors favor it] Mr. Treppass accompanies the narrator to the interview with the Governor and assists with interpretation. He believes that a larger deputation carrying presents and official authority might have produced a better effect, and that many Moors favor abolition.

The anti-slavery mission sought to persuade the Sultan and Moroccan authorities to consider an address against slavery. The narrator is told that the mission might have appeared more effective with stronger official backing, several delegates, presents, and letters from the Bey of Tunis.

l: abolition of slavery, Travels in Morocco
s: The Governor says that the Sultan will not accept abolition through persuasion, while Mr. Treppass believes that a considerable number of Moors support it. The narrator suggests that abolition by the Turkish Sultan could influence Morocco.

The Governor says that the Koran does not command the liberation of slaves, although it commends those who voluntarily free them. He acknowledges divisions among Muslims over the subject and says that most people in his community oppose abolition.

l: Bey of Tunis, Travels in Morocco
s: The Bey of Tunis is a Muslim ruler who supports the suppression of slavery through engagements with Christians. He exercises broad authority: administering justice morning and evening at Kairwan, directing plaintiffs, seizing camels when needed, ordering punishment, and controlling Arabs' water management for the camp. He possesses and receives many camels, including compensation for tribal manslaughter, and remits duty for a Sicilian nobleman's exported camels. During travel to Kairwan and onward toward Gilma and Ghafsa, he inspects arriving Arabs, exchanges gifts of horses and other presents, replaces a criticized grey horse, hunts and hawks, orders water released from Wady Tuckah, and keeps fifty Turks guarding the ruined Kasbah at Ghafsa.

l: Imaum of Muscat, Travels in Morocco
s: supports abolition of slavery [through an engagement with Christians] The Imaum of Muscat is cited alongside the Bey of Tunis as a Muslim ruler who has entered into engagements with Christians for the suppression of slavery. The Governor explains that their views differ from those held in Morocco.

commends abolition of slavery [as a voluntary act, not as a commanded duty] The Governor denies that the Koran commands the abolition of slavery. He says that it commends Muslims who voluntarily liberate their slaves and promises them God's blessing.

Jereed, also called Belad-el-Jereed and properly called the Tunisian Sahara, is a country of dates in the Tunisian portion of the Sahara near the Great Desert. Once occupied by Carthaginians and then Romans, as antiquities show, it contains Toser, its headquarters, Nefta and other date oases, and El-Sibhah, a vast salt lake or plain. It is largely flat, dry, sparsely inhabited, and marked by little water, ruins, Arab encampments, hunting plains, palm gardens, and warm watercourses. Date palms surround its towns; dates and palm products are its principal resources, with dates judged better than those of Ghabs. A single rainy day in the past year was linked to their ripeness. About twenty thousand people live entirely on dates for six months, while trade and tribute in dates, money, woollen goods, blankets, quilts, and animals support the Bey and Government. Sidi Mohammed, Captain Balfour, and Richard Reade traveled there, and tourists later carried away its baskets, dates, skins, woollen articles, and live animals.

El-Sibhah, also called Sibhah-el-Soudeeat, is a vast salt lake or salt plain in El-Jereed. Extending about seventy English miles north-east to south-west, it has seasonally changing dry islands and a hard central salt surface. Its agreeable salt is weaker than sea salt and is neither exported nor commercially used.

Toser is a town in the Jereed, identified with ancient Tisurus, with about six thousand people and surrounding villages behind a mud wall. Though poor in appearance, it has mosques, schools, baths, inns, markets, and brick and mud dwellings often built from Roman ruins. Its greatest wealth is its abundant watered date gardens and finest-quality dates, alongside household weaving of burnouses. Its wells are insufficient, so it relies on Wad Meshra. Travelers calculated it at 200 miles from Ghabs; its dates were later taken as tribute.

Nefta, ancient Negeta, is a southern frontier town of the Tunisian territories, about fourteen miles from Toser.
