Villages divided by gardens, supplied by Wad Nefta, contain mosques, schools, markets, saints, merchants, proprietors, and Shereefs. Ruled through its Shereefs, it is the gate of Tunis and an intermediary for Gulf-region caravan trade toward the Sahara.

Ghafsa is a town at the foot of hills beside an extensive plain, surrounded by olive and date trees. Though largely ruined and dirty, it has numerous hot mineral springs, ancient baths, gardens, and a nearly ruined Kasbah built chiefly from ancient remains. Its water irrigates the plain and supports palms and olives; local people make olive oil by hand. On a return march to Tunis, a party reached Ghafsa after rain, hail, high wind, and severe cold; Ghabs was about 130 miles away.

Dates are the principal food and resource of El-Jereed, sustaining twenty thousand people in Jereed for six months each year. Harvested in considerable quantities, though fine kinds are not abundant, they are stored in suspended bunches, pressed into earthen jars for syrup, or dried and ground into durable meal for desert travellers. Large arrivals include sweet transparent Degalah, plum-like Trungah, and larger, drier, less-sweet Monachah. Rain harms the fruit, while the trees’ roots need abundant water.

is_a plantations of date-palms [beautiful landscape features] Palm-groves are described as beautiful plantations whose trees are generally planted in a quincunx or at distances of four or five yards apart. They are commonly situated beside streams or rivulets, and abundant water produces healthier trees and finer fruit. The groves may yield very large quantities of dates, with one plantation producing fifteen hundred camels' loads.

Irrigation is essential to date-palms: in spring and summer, small channels carry stream water to tree basins, where clay embankments retain it until it soaks into earth; palms tolerate salt, sweet, or nitre-impregnated water.

requires irrigation [in spring and throughout summer] Date cultivation requires regular watering at the roots every four or five days and the removal of lower branches when they droop or wither. The palms are usually propagated from shoots, and the male plants are hung or shaken over the female plants in February or March to ensure fruitfulness. Excessive rain injures the dates, although the trees thrive in generally dry countries.

is_based_on dates [principal resource of El-Jereed] Dates are exported from El-Jereed to other parts of the Regency and to foreign countries because of their fine quality. The average annual export is stated as three to four thousand quintals. The produce of a large plantation may be sold for one thousand dollars.

is_conducted_by Bey of the Camp [through the flying-camp] Tribute collection is one of the duties associated with governing El-Jereed and the other divisions of the Regency. It is carried out through a yearly visit by a flying camp led by the Bey of the Camp.

tour_in the Jereed The tourists traveled with the Bey's expedition, carrying their baggage on three camels and staying in a tent near the Bey's. They visited the Bey, observed the camp's organization and customs, hunted extensively, and received his presents and hospitality.
Captain Balfour, a tourist on the Jereed tour, prefers Trungah dates; joining Richard Reade, he narrowly avoids a ceremonial-gun wad, hunts, and observes camp life.

l: Bey of the Camp, Travels in Morocco
s: The Bey of the Camp is the heir-apparent to the Tunisian throne and sovereign in the Jereed during his annual flying-camp. Accompanied by officers, ministers, and mamelukes, he visits El-Jereed to administer affairs, collect tribute, and hold justice morning and evening from a palace at Toser. He receives gifts, shoots at targets, decorates horses, and punishes or imprisons people in disputes involving tribute and alleged theft. His exactions on tribes may have contributed to an attack on couriers, though tourists describe him as hospitable and kind. He owns Momakeeah and surrounding land. When the reigning Bey dies, he takes the hereditary beylick and nominates a successor.

l: Tour to the Jereed, Travels in Morocco
s: A narrative tour, drawn from tourists’ notebooks and the author’s observations, gives details of the Jereed region, including Toser, Nefta, and Ghafsa. It follows Captain Balfour and Richard Reade across plains and hills toward Kairwan, encountering ruins, villages, wildlife, and severe daily temperature changes.

l: the expedition and camp, Travels in Morocco
s: The Bey’s camp, used for tribute collection, comprised about 2,660 people: Mamelukes, 300 Turkish Infantry, Spahis, roughly 2,000 Arab camp followers, attendants, two artillery pieces, and about 2,000 camels. Tents surrounded the Bey’s central tent, with water supplied from Tunis. The expedition marched ten to twenty miles at a time through varied country, encamping near several places and gaining Arabs. Along the way members hunted, bathed, inspected ruins and houses, and observed local natural features.

Richard Reade, eldest son of Sir Thomas Reade, was a tourist on the tour to the Jereed. He joined Captain Balfour’s expedition, received a hyaena skin and head and a bay horse from the Bey of Tunis, and visited Kairwan. He hunted and observed local customs, reported an insult, then pleaded successfully for the Arab’s protection.

Turkish Infantry were 300 irregular Turkish troops in the expedition, arriving two hours after mounted troops, honored by the Bey, performing sword fights and music, guarding camp nightly, and shouting 'Alleya.'

l: the plain of Manouba, Travels in Morocco
s: The Bey crossed the plain of Manouba after leaving the Bardo. It was covered by baggage-camels, horses, mules, attendants, and troops moving in what the tourists called glorious confusion.

Kairwan is a clean city with many ruined houses and much of a regiment of the Nitham quartered there. After an expedition crossed sparsely inhabited, water-poor hills, it appeared beyond them beside a boundless plain toward Susa; the party then visited its holy well, fortress, Kaed's house, and Bey's place of justice.

Algiers is included in the middle Western Region and in the mountain system extending across the Barbary States. The Pass of Teniah, leading from Algiers to Mediah, is treated as part of the principal mountain chain in that area.

l: the Bey's expedition, Travels in Morocco
s: The Bey's expedition, with mounted guards, Turkish Infantry, artillery, followers, animals, and attendants, passes through Manouba and travels south through the Jereed, repeatedly breaking camp, marching, saluting, hunting, and encamping.

The march proceeded at about four miles per hour, with mounted troops ahead, infantry and camels following, and water carried from Tunis. The Bey saluted guards and soldiers, hunted off-route, and returned to the next encampment.

The bastinado is a generally formal punishment intended as terror, inflicted on tied culprits’ soles. Against Arabs accused of stealing barley, inferior Mamelukes beat them, though many strokes were omitted or merely taps or scratches.

l: the administration of justice, Travels in Morocco
s: The Bey heard many plaintiffs in Kairwan, issuing redress orders or referrals to kadys and chiefs, while summarily dismissing many; no defendants appeared.

l: the water supply, Travels in Morocco
s: originates_in Tunis [carried to camp by camels] Water was scarce throughout much of the route and limited cultivation and habitation. The Bey's personal water was brought from Tunis by camels, while the camp relied on streams, wells, and water found near Arab encampments; a missing bridge arch could have forced a thirty-mile detour if the stream had risen.

A wild animal abundant in the forests of the Morocco Atlas, the hyaena is described as generally stupid and not usually dangerous; it was flushed, shot by Si Smyle, and its skin and head were sent to Richard Reade.

Gazelles are swift small deer, faster than greyhounds and difficult to catch. During marches near Gilma, they were repeatedly encountered and pursued; some were caught by Arabs or dogs, one escaped wounded, and Captain B. caught one.

Camels were scarce in Bedouin districts because a disorder caused great mortality, yet the Bey of Tunis possessed many and farmed them through overseers for mills and agricultural work; others were acquired through tribal fines for manslaughter. They were valued for crossing vast plains, though they could not supersede mules in Mediterranean islands. An expedition and camp had about two thousand camels, which carried no provender and lived on coarse grass, weeds, and thorns, especially sharp prickly thorns. Some bore women in enclosed palanquins, with bells and rigging that earned them the name “ship of the Desert.” On the return to Tunis, clayey ground prevented many from reaching camp, and 550 died. Prices ranged from 60 to 200 piastres.

l: the hunting and shooting, Travels in Morocco
s: The Bey hunted every day and was described as a highly accurate shot from horseback, killing partridges and other game. The tourists and their companions pursued wild boar, hyaenas, foxes, wolves, hares, partridges, and gazelles, though difficult terrain, the speed of the animals, and poor preparation limited their success.
The famous mosque at Kairwan, inaccessible to R.'s party, was said by Giovanni to contain marble pillars and ornaments taken from Christian churches and Pagan temples.

l: house of the Kaed, Travels in Morocco
s: is_a dwelling [good specimen of dwellings in the country] The house of the Kaed was described as a good specimen of dwellings in the country. R. and his companions visited it, ate sweetmeats and dinner there, and later returned to it after visiting the holy well.

The old Kaed was ill and weeping because his son, who commanded part of the camp guards, had arrived. He was described as a great fanatic, and his mamelukes stopped R. from approaching him for fear that R. might be insulted.

l: Sidi Amour Abeda, Travels in Morocco
s: Sidi Amour Abeda is a Moorish saint treated as a man of exceeding sanctity. On a ride to Kairwan, he accompanies R.'s party to the Kaed's house, blesses sweetmeats, receives reverent hand-kissing, and is promised a burial house by order of the Bey.
Moorish saints are numerous in Kairwan, defined by descent from the Prophet and lucky divination; they receive devout obeisance while exploiting poor people.

Santa Maria is a Frenchman travelling with the Bey’s party, experienced in North Africa and fluent in Arabic. After returning a horse to the Bey and receiving another, he is criticized for delicacy and impudence toward the Bey’s officers. Assigned by the Bey of the Camp to espionage, he leaves for Ghabs with twelve men, returns safely, and is praised as enterprising. He then goes to Beja to report, planning later visits to Tripoli and Ghadames.

l: Bey's ministers and mamelukes, Travels in Morocco
s: serve Bey of Tunis [guards and attendants] Mamelukes stopped R. when he ran up to shake hands with the old Kaed, fearing that the Kaed might insult him. They also served the Bey and dealt with the French officer's complaint about the grey horse.

l: Bey's camel seizure, Travels in Morocco
s: After disorder caused heavy camel mortality and scarcity, parties for the Bey seized about two hundred of the finest camels, marked them taba as government property, despite former owners' cries and curses.

Hares were found in large numbers in warrens and among tufts of rushy grass, and many were caught with dogs or hawks. When attacked by hawks, a hare sometimes ran briefly, dodged the bird's pounce, or hid in grass or a bush before being driven out by Arabs.

has_water_resources springs [described as bountiful but neglected by people] The Desert contains abundant but neglected water, including springs and streams that could support extensive irrigation. Its landscape includes hot springs, salt-covered plains, sparse grasses, thorny plants, date groves, and striking scenery.

l: hot springs of Ghafsa, Travels in Morocco
s: The hot springs of Ghafsa are hot, sulphurous, and other mineral waters near ancient bath structures and inscription fragments. Observed at ninety-five degrees, they contain fish resembling gudgeons and small snakes that live together; the snakes feed entirely on the fish.

l: falconry and hunting, Travels in Morocco
s: Hawks caught hobaras, hares, and other birds during the expedition, although strong wind sometimes prevented them from being flown. Dogs caught hares, gazelles, and a fox, while Arabs and members of the expedition also shot or pursued game. The hawks used in hunting hares had their legs connected by a leather strap to prevent strain when one claw seized the hare and the other caught the ground.

l: water management in the desert, Travels in Morocco
s: Water management in the desert is controlled by the Bey through orders to district Arabs. At Wady Tuckah, water is released from the hills and directed to camp through tanks, cisterns, ducts, pools, streams, and springs. Though abundant enough to irrigate plains and support palms and olives, it is neglected.

l: date cultivation and trade at Toser, Travels in Morocco
s: Toser’s abundantly irrigated date gardens produce prized dates, the inhabitants’ near-exclusive food; stones cover streets, and the Bey taxes each tree at two bunches.
